item.title: FEO pulls down premature election date release from its website
item.description: The Fijian Elections Office has removed a press release from its website that prematurely announced the issuance of the Writ of Election for the 2026 General Election. An FEO spokesperson said the press release was prepared as part of a mock exercise and should not have been uploaded to the website.
item.content:encoded:
The Fijian Elections Office has removed a press release from its website that prematurely announced the issuance of the Writ of Election for the 2026 General Election.

An FEO spokesperson said the press release was prepared as part of a mock exercise and should not have been uploaded to the website.

The release, which had been online for about 12 hours as at 8am this morning, stated that the Electoral Commission and FEO had confirmed the formal commencement of the 2026 General Election following the issuance of the Writ of Election by President Ratu Naiqama Lalabalavu at State House.

It further stated that the election would be held on Tuesday, September 22, 2026, with polling stations open from 7.30am to 6pm.

The mock release also stated that Fiji had a provisional 707,982 registered voters as of August 9, comprising 355,500 female voters and 352,482 male voters.

The FEO has clarified that the release was part of an exercise and was not an official announcement of the issuance of the Writ of Election or the election date.

item.title: Usamate calls on PM to reconsider Singh’s return to sugar portfolio
item.description: Opposition Member of Parliament Jone Usamate has criticised the decision to return the Sugar portfolio to Charan Jeath Singh, saying cane farmers cannot afford what he describes as a return to failed leadership and unfulfilled promises. Usamate said he was concerned that Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka had again handed responsibility for the sugar industry to Singh, months after he was moved from t
item.content:encoded:
Opposition Member of Parliament Jone Usamate has criticised the decision to return the Sugar portfolio to Charan Jeath Singh, saying cane farmers cannot afford what he describes as a return to failed leadership and unfulfilled promises.

Usamate said he was concerned that Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka had again handed responsibility for the sugar industry to Singh, months after he was moved from the portfolio.

“It is with great concern that the Prime Minister has once again handed the Sugar portfolio to Hon. Charan Jeath Singh, barely months after he was moved out of it,” Usamate said.

“I believe this decision is a mistake and one that our cane farmers can ill afford.”

Usamate said Singh previously held the Sugar portfolio from December 2022 until January this year but, in his assessment, failed to deliver the meaningful changes promised to farmers.

“In that time, I did not see the meaningful change our farmers were promised. Instead, his tenure was marked by a fractured relationship with growers and industry stakeholders,” he said.

Usamate pointed to the National Farmers Union’s public reaction to Singh’s earlier removal from the portfolio and problems experienced at the Lautoka Mill, including an extended shutdown following a boiler tube leak.

He also questioned progress towards delivering a new modern sugar mill, saying farmers continued to depend on ageing milling infrastructure despite repeated announcements.

“For over a year now, we have heard talk after talk about a new, modern sugar mill for our farmers. Tenders were called, delegations travelled to India, Colombia and beyond and Cabinet ministers made one announcement after another,” Usamate said.

He said farmers were continuing to crush cane using ageing mills despite acknowledgement from the Prime Minister that replacement parts were no longer available for some of the equipment and that the mills had reached the end of their operational life.

“All the travel and all the press conferences under Mr Singh’s watch delivered talk, not tonnes, and not a new mill,” Usamate said.

He questioned what Singh would do differently after returning to the portfolio.

“I ask the Prime Minister: what has changed? What new plan does Mr Singh now bring to the table that he did not already try and fail to deliver in his first three years in the role?”

Usamate said the sugar industry remained critical to the livelihoods of nearly 200,000 people and needed leadership capable of rebuilding confidence among growers and delivering promised reforms.

“Our sugar industry and the nearly 200,000 people who depend on it deserve a Minister who can rebuild trust with farmers and actually deliver the modernisation this industry has been promised for years, not a return to the same fractured relationships and unfulfilled announcements,” he said.

Usamate called on Rabuka to reverse the decision.

“I call on the Prime Minister to reconsider this reappointment and to prioritise the interests of our cane farmers over political convenience,” he said.

item.title: Judge allows access to frozen funds
item.description: The High Court in Suva has ordered the immediate release of $150,000 from a frozen BRED Bank account belonging to Raijieli Naituku Chand, ruling that funds were needed to support the respondents and their family and meet medical needs. Acting Justice Penijamini R. Lomaloma made the order on August 6 in proceedings brought by the Fiji Independent Commission Against Corruption against Stephen Shalen
item.content:encoded:
The High Court in Suva has ordered the immediate release of $150,000 from a frozen BRED Bank account belonging to Raijieli Naituku Chand, ruling that funds were needed to support the respondents and their family and meet medical needs.

Acting Justice Penijamini R. Lomaloma made the order on August 6 in proceedings brought by the Fiji Independent Commission Against Corruption against Stephen Shalen Chand and hius wife, Raijieli Naituku Chand.

The ruling varies an earlier freezing order imposed on the account, which the court said holds more than $1.3 million.

“The Respondents need to survive,” Acting Justice Lomaloma said.

The court was told that Stephen Chand has a serious medical condition requiring overseas surgery and uses electronic equipment to monitor his condition.

The judgment states that the equipment was in FICAC’s possession and that criminal charges had not been laid against Chand at the time of the ruling.

The court was also told the respondents were supporting several grandchildren, nephews and nieces and did not have another source of income.

“The Respondents and their family need money to survive and meet their daily needs,” Acting Justice Lomaloma found.

“Justice requires that some funds need to be released to the Respondents to meet these needs.”

The court ordered BRED Bank to immediately release $150,000 to Raijieli Chand from her account.

However, the remaining funds will continue to be frozen, with the bank prohibited from allowing any withdrawal, transfer, payment, disposal, encumbrance or other dealing without a further court order.

Acting Justice Lomaloma also ordered FICAC to immediately return all medical equipment belonging to Stephen Chand that was in the commission’s possession.

The case stems from proceedings filed by FICAC in May seeking to have a property at Domain Road in Nasese declared “tainted property” under the Proceeds of Crime Act 1997 and ultimately forfeited to the State, subject to a mortgage.

The court said evidence showed about $322,468.09 had been received by Stephen Chand, while more than $1.3 million was held in the frozen account belonging to Raijieli Chand.

Acting Justice Lomaloma noted that the restraining order had been obtained on the lower legal threshold that there were “reasonable grounds for suspecting that the property is tainted property.”

Stephen and Raijieli Chand have filed an application seeking to have the earlier injunctive orders dissolved.

That application was due to be heard on August 6, but FICAC told the court it was not ready to file its affidavit in opposition.

Acting Justice Lomaloma said a separate hearing date would be set for that application.

The $150,000 release and return of the medical equipment take effect immediately, while the remainder of the funds remain subject to the court’s restraining order.

item.title: Internet banking uptake remains below half among connected Fijians
item.description: Less than half of Fijians with formal financial accounts and internet access have signed up for internet banking, despite widespread access to digital connectivity, according to the Fiji Financial Services Demand Side Survey 2025. The survey found that 74 per cent of formal financial account holders have access to the internet, with mobile data accounting for 89 per cent of connections.
item.content:encoded:
Less than half of Fijians with formal financial accounts and internet access have signed up for internet banking, despite widespread access to digital connectivity, according to the Fiji Financial Services Demand Side Survey 2025.

The survey found that 74 per cent of formal financial account holders have access to the internet, with mobile data accounting for 89 per cent of connections.

However, only 41 per cent of those with internet access had signed up for internet banking.

The survey identified a lack of awareness about the availability of internet banking services and uncertainty about how to use them as key barriers to uptake.

Despite relatively low registration, usage among those who have adopted internet banking is high.

The survey found that 87 per cent of people who had signed up for internet banking had used the service during the previous 12 months.

There is also significant potential for further growth, with 44 per cent of current non-users indicating they would be interested in using internet banking or a mobile banking application in the future, particularly for paying bills and transferring money.

The findings also reveal differences in access to and use of payment cards.

Sixty-eight per cent of Fijians with formal financial accounts have some form of payment card, while 67 per cent have a local debit card.

Among people who personally own a bank account, local debit card ownership increases to 83 per cent.

Women are significantly less likely than men to own local debit cards, with ownership recorded at 61 per cent for women compared with 72 per cent for men.

Card usage also differs between men and women.

Local debit cards are used an average of 3.1 times during a typical month, increasing to 3.4 times among male cardholders and falling to 2.7 times among women.

International debit cards remain considerably less common, with just 12 per cent of formal financial account holders owning one.

Ownership is higher among young people, urban residents and university-educated Fijians. The survey found 33 per cent of university-educated respondents had an international debit card.

Credit card penetration remains particularly low, with only three per cent of Fijians with formal financial accounts owning one.

The survey also identified a shift in the types of cards being used by banked Fijians since 2020.

Local debit card ownership among banked Fijians has fallen from 94 per cent in 2020 to 83 per cent in 2025.

In contrast, international debit card ownership increased from three per cent to 14 per cent, while credit card ownership rose from one per cent to four per cent among banked Fijians.

The findings indicate that while internet connectivity and access to formal financial services are relatively widespread, further work is required to improve awareness and adoption of digital banking services.

item.title: Niraj Bhartu appointed CEO at Vision Investments Fiji
item.description: The Board of Directors of Vision Investments Limited has appointed Niraj Bhartu as Chief Executive Officer, effective September 1, 2026, after he served a year in the acting position. Bhartu has been Acting CEO since September 1, 2025, and has more than a decade of service with the company.
item.content:encoded:
The Board of Directors of Vision Investments Limited has appointed Niraj Bhartu as Chief Executive Officer, effective September 1, 2026, after he served a year in the acting position.

Bhartu has been Acting CEO since September 1, 2025, and has more than a decade of service with the company.

Before taking up the acting CEO position, he served as General Manager Finance from 2015.

The Board said Bhartu brings more than 25 years of experience spanning executive management, finance, governance, risk, assurance and corporate advisory.

His extensive involvement across the Group has also provided him with a strong understanding of its diversified businesses, operations and key stakeholders.

Chairman Navin Patel said Bhartu was well positioned to guide the organisation through its next stage of development.

Patel described him as a “highly experienced and capable executive” who would lead the company and Group into their “next phase of growth, diversification and transformation.”

Bhartu holds a Bachelor of Arts degree in Accounting and Information Systems from the University of the South Pacific and a Master of Professional Accounting from the University of Western Sydney.

He is a Fellow of CPA Australia, a Chartered Accountant and member of the Fiji Institute of Chartered Accountants, and a member of the Australian Institute of Company Directors.

Bhartu is also an alumnus of the Leadership Fiji Programme and has completed executive education programmes at the Indian Institute of Management Bangalore.

In 2018, he was named Listed Company Achiever of the Year at the SPX Grand Awards.

item.title: Constitution must rise above political camps – Dialogue Fiji
item.description: A Constitution should not be treated as a political party manifesto or used as a test of loyalty to a particular political camp, says Dialogue Fiji Executive Director Nilesh Lal. Speaking at the launch of two constitutional literacy publications in Suva, Lal said Fiji needed to move away from highly politicised constitutional debates and towards examining what constitutional provisions actually sa
item.content:encoded:
A Constitution should not be treated as a political party manifesto or used as a test of loyalty to a particular political camp, says Dialogue Fiji Executive Director Nilesh Lal.

Speaking at the launch of two constitutional literacy publications in Suva, Lal said Fiji needed to move away from highly politicised constitutional debates and towards examining what constitutional provisions actually say.

“A Constitution should not be treated like a political party manifesto. It should not become a tribal badge or a test of loyalty to one political camp,” Lal said.

“It belongs to the entire country, including those who disagree with the government of the day and those who may never support the political actors responsible for producing it.”

Lal said while the process through which a Constitution was developed remained extremely important, its history and authorship should not replace proper scrutiny of its contents.

He said questions should instead focus on how a Constitution distributes power, protects rights, establishes Parliament, appoints independent institutions, controls the Executive and can be amended.

Lal said Fijians often held strong opinions about different constitutions without necessarily knowing what those documents actually contained.

“People will very staunchly tell you that a particular Constitution is good or that another Constitution is bad,” he said.

“Yet when you turn around and ask them what exactly in the Constitution is good, or which particular provisions are bad, they often have no clue.”

He said political allegiance was consequently influencing how some people viewed Fiji’s constitutional frameworks.

“Whatever the politicians they support tell them about a constitution shapes their opinion of it. If their preferred political leaders say a Constitution is good, then it is good. If those political leaders say it is bad, then it is bad.”

“People judge a Constitution according to who produced it, rather than examining what the document actually provides.”

Dialogue Fiji has launched two publications comparing Fiji’s recent constitutional frameworks and explaining constitutional issues in simpler language.

The first, Fiji’s Recent Constitutional Frameworks: Comparing the 1997 Constitution, the Ghai Draft, and the 2013 Constitution , places the major provisions of the three frameworks side by side.

It compares areas including Bills of Rights, electoral systems, Parliament, the Executive, Judiciary, accountability institutions and constitutional amendment procedures.

The second publication, Understanding Fiji’s Recent Constitutions: A Citizen’s Illustrated Guide , is designed for ordinary citizens and uses illustrations, comparative tables and plain-language explanations.

Lal stressed that the publications do not endorse one constitutional framework over another but are intended to allow people to assess individual provisions themselves.

He said Fiji needed constitutional discussions based on knowledge rather than political division.

“We need people to debate constitutional provisions from a place of knowledge, rather than from the current toxic, highly politicised and highly polarising discourse surrounding the Constitution,” Lal said.

He said disagreement was expected and healthy in a democracy, but it should be based on what constitutional texts actually provide rather than “political slogans, misinformation and blind loyalty to particular political leaders”.

Lal said improving constitutional literacy was particularly important for Fiji because of its history of coups, political instability, authoritarian governance and the abrogation and rewriting of constitutions.

“For Fiji, constitutional literacy is not simply an academic exercise. It is essential to the protection and survival of our democracy,” he said.

Deputy Prime Minister Manoa Kamikamica formally launched the publications in Suva.

item.title: Old Fiji banknotes to lose legal tender status from January
item.description: Businesses will no longer be required to accept Fiji’s old flora and fauna banknotes as payment after December 31, 2026, as the Reserve Bank of Fiji moves to complete the transition to the country’s new polymer currency. The RBF said the old-design banknotes have now been gazetted for demonetisation, effective January 1, 2027.
item.content:encoded:
Businesses will no longer be required to accept Fiji’s old flora and fauna banknotes as payment after December 31, 2026, as the Reserve Bank of Fiji moves to complete the transition to the country’s new polymer currency.

The RBF said the old-design banknotes have now been gazetted for demonetisation, effective January 1, 2027.

This means the old notes can continue to be used for payments until the end of this year, but businesses will not be obliged to accept them for goods and services from January 1.

The move follows the introduction of Fiji’s new polymer banknotes into circulation on January 2 this year.

RBF Governor Ariff Ali said a significant proportion of the old currency had already been removed from circulation.

As of July 31, 72.3 per cent of the old banknotes in circulation had been recalled.

Ali acknowledged members of the public for supporting what he described as a smooth and gradual transition to the new polymer notes.

He said recalling old banknotes was an important process for central banks as it helped prevent public confusion, maintain the quality of banknotes in circulation and reduce counterfeiting risks.

The RBF has reminded people who still hold old flora and fauna banknotes to take note of the December 31 deadline.

The demonetisation forms part of Fiji’s transition from the previous flora and fauna series to the new polymer banknotes introduced at the beginning of 2026.

item.title: COI judgment deferred to Friday
item.description: The High Court judgment on legal challenges to findings of the Commission of Inquiry into the appointment of former FICAC Commissioner Barbara Malimali has been deferred to Friday. Justice Dane Tuiqereqere told the parties this afternoon that the ruling was not ready, noting that the decision would be “particularly long”.
item.content:encoded:
The High Court judgment on legal challenges to findings of the Commission of Inquiry into the appointment of former FICAC Commissioner Barbara Malimali has been deferred to Friday.

Justice Dane Tuiqereqere told the parties this afternoon that the ruling was not ready, noting that the decision would be “particularly long”.

The matters have now been adjourned to 2.30pm on Friday, August 14, with Justice Tuiqereqere saying he would do his best to complete the judgment by then.

The judicial review proceedings involve former FICAC Commissioner Barbara Malimali, former Attorney-General Graham Leung, Fiji Law Society president Wylie Clarke and lawyer Laurel Vaurasi.

The four applicants have separately challenged findings made against them arising from the Commission of Inquiry into Malimali’s appointment as Commissioner of the Fiji Independent Commission Against Corruption.

Malimali’s proceeding, HBJ 09/2025, names the Commission of Inquiry, the President, the Prime Minister and the Attorney-General as respondents. She is represented by Waqanika Law.

A separate proceeding, HBJ 10/2025, has been brought by Clarke and Vaurasi, who have also named the Commission of Inquiry, the President, the Prime Minister and the Attorney-General as respondents. They are represented by Howards Lawyers.

Leung’s proceeding, HBJ 11/2025, names the Commission of Inquiry and the Attorney-General as respondents. He is represented by Fatiaki Law.

The judgment is expected to determine the legal challenges brought by the four applicants over findings concerning them in the Commission of Inquiry report.

The Commission was established to investigate the circumstances surrounding Malimali’s appointment as FICAC Commissioner.

All three matters will now return before Justice Tuiqereqere on Friday afternoon for the anticipated judgment.
